transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE), Lena Morales (Pegasus Head of ML), Rajesh Iyer (Product), Tom Wu (Eng Lead)

Summary (auto):
- Kickoff for POC focused on quality eval plan: golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination & format checks, scoring approach, workload sizing and timelines.
- Agreed deliverables and due dates; plan first benchmark run by end of month.

Topics:
- Golden prompt definition and templating
- Regression test harness and expected outputs
- Hallucination detection heuristics / format validation
- Scoring: weighted metrics (format, factuality, latency, cost)
- Workload sizing: burst vs steady, 5k initial, scale tests
- Timeline and gating for Dedicated vs Hosted decisions

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: okay everyone thanks for joining, um this is Alex from Redwood, i'll hand it off to Samir in a sec to run through the technical plan but wanted to set context, this call is to scope the POC eval — golden prompts, regression tests and how we score.
[00:18] Lena: hey thanks Alex, ya from Pegasus we care most about output format (we have downstream parsers) and hallucinations, those are the two blockers for launch.
[00:30] Rajesh: and timeline is tight — quarter end push so we need a quick go/no-go within two weeks of the run.
[00:40] Samir: got it, so propose a two-phase eval: phase 1 is correctness & format (golden prompts + format checks), phase 2 is robustness at scale including hallucination detection and latency/cost tradeoffs.
[01:05] Tom: quick question — when you say golden prompts, do you mean a single canonical prompt per workflow or a set of variants?
[01:15] Samir: good question, we recommend a small set: 5–10 golden prompts that represent typical user intents, plus 30–50 variants to test prompt brittleness. so canonical + variants.
[01:30] Lena: sounds reasonable. we already have about 1k historical human messages, we can pick 200 as candidates. we'll anonymize.
[01:45] Alex: excellent. on the scoring side we usually do a weighted rubric: format pass/fail (heavily weighted), factuality/hallucination score, semantic similarity / BLEU-like for optional fields, and latency/cost as secondary metrics.
[02:05] Rajesh: can you give an example weighting?
[02:12] Alex: typically something like format 40%, hallucination/factuality 35%, semantic 15%, latency/cost 10%. but configurable.
[02:25] Lena: format 40 feels right, because if downstream parsers fail we're blocked.
[02:35] Samir: for hallucination detection we'll run both automated heuristics and human review on a sample. heuristics include exact-match checks against known facts, NER cross-checks, and a provenance flag when the model emits citations. also fuzzy checks for numbers/dates.
[02:55] Tom: about the "provenance flag" — our dataset sometimes lacks ground-truth for certain facts; how do you score those?
[03:05] Samir: good point — those would be marked as "unknown" and excluded from strict factuality scoring; we can still evaluate hallucination patterns (e.g., made-up entities) and treat them as a separate metric.
[03:18] Lena: we want an explicit hallucination threshold — our legal folks asked for < 2% on critical flows.
[03:28] Alex: we'll put that in the success criteria. what's reasonable for format acceptance?
[03:34] Rajesh: 98% of structured outputs must validate against our schema.
[03:40] Samir: ok format >=98, hallucination <2 as initial gates.
[03:45] [small crosstalk, inaudible] Speaker 1: uh yeah
[03:55] Samir: for regression tests we suggest creating a test harness with deterministic checks: golden prompts should always produce the same structured shape; any deviation is a regression. we'll version-check model outputs across model variants and quantization levels.
[04:18] Tom: does Redwood support running these tests across multiple model variants automatically?
[04:25] Samir: yes — Redwood's test harness can run parallel jobs against hosted and dedicated endpoints, and we can compare outputs side-by-side. though if you go Dedicated we'll need to provision capacity — that affects timeline.
[04:40] Lena: talk to me about workload sizing — we have peak bursts of 200 TPS for some customers but typically 20–40 TPS. for the POC what do you recommend?
[04:55] Alex: for initial quality eval we do a steady 5k prompt batch to cover coverage; then a simulated burst test at your peak of 200 TPS for ~10 minutes to validate latency SLOs and autoscale policies.
[05:12] Rajesh: 5k seems fine. are tokens counted? cost sizing?
[05:18] Alex: yes we'll estimate token counts from your 1k sample and extrapolate. Samir will run a token profile and give cost estimates per 1k, 5k, and 50k runs.
[05:30] Samir: i'll add quantization/FP16 vs int8 variants into the run matrix so you can see cost vs quality tradeoffs.
[05:40] Lena: do you include prefix / KV cache testing? we rely heavily on session context.
[05:46] Samir: we'll run prefix-heavy sequences in phase 2, including KV cache hit/miss analysis. some of the runtime optimizations are architecture-specific so we'll note performance differences per GPU type.
[05:58] Alex: i'm going to recap success criteria so we all align: format >=98%, hallucination <2% on critical flows, average latency under 600ms p50 for typical prompt size, and cost per 1k within your target (we'll compute). if any gate fails we run targeted tuning (prompt adjustments, quantization profile, or change model family).
[06:28] Tom: what about human-in-the-loop? do you expect us to do adjudication?
[06:33] Samir: yes we ask for a small human review panel — we'll sample 200 outputs for manual labeling to calibrate automated detectors. that helps set thresholds and reduces false positives.
[06:45] Rajesh: who owns labeling? Pegasus or Redwood?
[06:50] Alex: typically customer provides labels for domain-specific checks; Redwood can help with annotation if needed as an optional service.
[06:58] Lena: we'll handle initial labeling.
[07:02] Samir: operationally the harness will produce a per-prompt JSON with fields: prompt_id, model_variant, output, format_valid (bool), hallucination_flag (bool), hallucination_reason (if any), semantic_score, latency_ms, token_cost. note: some field names might be transcribed wrong in this recording, but we'll push a schema.
[07:30] Rajesh: we need the scoring rubric to be human-readable — product and legal will want to see how numbers map to pass/fail.
[07:40] Alex: will do. rubric will include examples of common failure modes and a short adjudication guide.
[07:50] Lena: about timelines — you said Samir can share harness by Friday?
[07:54] Samir: yes i'll share the repo + runbook by 2025-06-21.
[07:58] Alex: Alex to share pricing and POC contract template by 2025-06-20.
[08:03] Tom: one more technical: how do you detect hallucinated numeric values like dates/amounts? we have lots of financial numbers.
[08:12] Samir: we run numeric consistency checks against source fields when available, range checks, and cross-field dependency rules. plus heuristic detectors trained to flag invented names and dates. none are perfect but combined with the human sample it's effective.
[08:30] Rajesh: ok, in terms of gating for Dedicated vs Hosted — what triggers that?
[08:36] Alex: typically volume and compliance. if during the POC your per-second throughput or data residency needs require VPC, we discuss Dedicated. but initial quality eval can run on Hosted with a private dataset.
[08:50] Lena: compliance: we need SOC2 + SSO integration for anything beyond trials. are these available?
[08:57] Alex: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II, SAML SSO, KMS integrations for Private deployments. we'll share the security pack in the folder.
[09:08] [pause] Speaker 2: hmm
[09:12] Samir: for the sample test plan i'm proposing these concrete steps:
- collect 1k anonymized prompts from Pegasus (customer)
- identify 200 golden prompts across critical flows
- craft 30–50 variants per golden prompt for brittleness testing
- run 5k batch across three model variants (base, quantized, tuned)
- sample 200 outputs for human review for hallucination calibration
- run burst test at 200 TPS to check latency/scale
[09:48] Tom: do you also track output token length distribution?
[09:52] Samir: yes token distribution and tail latencies will be part of the report.
[09:58] Lena: what about regression tests for future model updates? we don't want surprise regressions when you patch runtime.
[10:04] Alex: good point — we'll set up a nightly regression job that runs golden prompts, and any failed regression will alert both teams. for POC we'll keep it daily.
[10:16] Rajesh: sounds good. who signs off on go/no-go?
[10:20] Lena: product + ML lead — so me and Tom, with Rajesh for product signoff.
[10:26] Alex: i'll note that.
[10:29] [small laughter] Speaker 3: ok
[10:34] Samir: any blockers we haven't covered?
[10:36] Tom: just access to the dataset and a shared S3 bucket, we need an upload path.
[10:42] Alex: we'll create a temporary secure bucket and share credentials; Tom you upload and let Samir know.
[10:48] Rajesh: also, how do you handle partial success? like format ok but hallucination slightly above threshold?
[10:55] Samir: we'll surface the breakdown per flow; if it's isolated to a subflow we can tune prompts or fall back to a safer model family on that flow. Redwood supports per-route model routing as a mitigation.
[11:10] Lena: good to know.
[11:14] Alex: okay i'm going to read back the next steps quickly: Alex sends pricing & rubric by 6/20; Samir shares harness + runbook by 6/21; Pegasus provides 1k anonymized prompts by 6/20; Samir runs token profiling and returns cost estimates; run scheduled and results by 6/30; follow-up review on 7/2.
[11:40] Lena: confirmed.
[11:42] Rajesh: confirmed.
[11:44] Tom: confirmed.
[11:46] Alex: great. anything else?
[11:48] [pause] Speaker 4: no
[11:50] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll also include an appendix of common hallucination examples and format failure examples in the shared folder.
[11:58] Samir: and i'll include a short example run output so you can see the JSON per-prompt record.
[12:05] Lena: appreciate it. talk soon.
[12:08] Alex: thanks all, bye.

End of meeting.
